figures.caption: Figure 1: (A) The AAC Pareto Frontier. Traditional AAC devices force a tradeoff [13] between expressivity (Communication Expressivity, y-axis) and efficiency (Communication Efficiency, x-axis). An example of Mechanism 1 is letter-by-letter typing, which captures nuance but is slow; and an example of Mechanism 2 is preset phrases, which are fast but potentially generic. We propose that Cognitive Alignment (CA)—achieved by grounding LLM generation on human intentionality—allows the frontier to be broken as illustrated. By successfully expanding compressed inputs (abbreviations) into the intended utterances, users will better achieve high expressivity without sacrificing efficiency. (B) Keyboard expansion and typing based on eye-gaze control. A combination of bi-gram and tri-gram allows the selection of letters via a keyboard expansion through directional gestures performed by eye movement. Additional high-frequency common words can be placed for easy access on the keyboard for positional gaze detection. (C) Contextual Steering. The CCI achieves CA by injecting multimodal context (visual ego-centric view, saliency, audio) and pragmatic elements (referents, motive of communication, emotion) into the LLM inference process. A test-time intervention mechanism (e.g. prompting or steering) uses these signals to steer the LLM, ensuring the abbreviation “A G U O T” is expanded into the contextually relevant utterances that steered closer to the intended phrase like (“A GOOD USE OF TIME") or (“ALWAYS GET UP ON TIME").

Figure 2: Frontier LLMs achieve up to ∼ 88% top-5 expansion accuracy when aligned to pragmatic context. (A) Image-Chat dataset. (Top) Illustration of the 4 layers. L0 includes no context information and simply asks the LLM to expand the abbreviated sentence. L1 includes the emotion of Speaker A (first dialogue line) and L2 further includes the emotion of Speaker B (second dialogue line). L3 includes referents and L4 the full scene description. (Bottom) Performance for Speaker A (first row) and Speaker B (second row) under different context layers (L0–L4), and in the emotion ablated condition 𝐿4\𝐿2. The y-axis represents Accuracy, and bars denote Top-1 and Top-5 performance. (B) Generated dataset. (Top) L0 is as in panel A. L1 includes the Motive of Communication (MOC), and L2 includes the speaker emotion and explicitness level. L3 includes target and distractor referents, and L4 the scene description. (Bottom) Performance across context layers and in the emotion ablated condition 𝐿4 \ 𝐿2. The y-axis represents Accuracy, and bars denote Top-1 and Top-5 performance. Statistical significance was assessed using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (one-sided) with Holm–Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. * p < .05, ** p < .01, *** p < .001.

Figure 3: Cognitive Steering - Prompting vs. test-time steering for alternative context layers. (A) Structured prompting is used to provide pragmatic context features (e.g., MOC, emotions, explicitness, referents) to the model at inference time. (B) Steering procedure: a context-direction vector is added to the residual stream of a chosen layer with varying strength (Steering 1–2), enabling alignment without modifying the prompt. Steering 1 steers layers 15, 20, and 25; Steering 2 steers layers 30, 35, and 38 (OLMo-2-13B-Instruct has 40 layers [21]). (C) Top-5 LLM-judged similarity for alternative steering approaches (bars) on the generated dataset benchmark, for L3 (MOC, emotions, explicitness) and L4 (+Referents) context layer. The y-axis represents Top-5 LLM-judged similarity. Statistical significance was assessed using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (one-sided) with Holm–Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. * p < .05, ** p < .01, *** p < .001.
